questions.prompt: Veld opens its economy to international trade. Which of the following is most likely to be a benefit for consumers in Veld?
hints: Think about the benefits of trade from the point of view of households, not firms or the government.
Check each option: is it actually a benefit, and does it go to consumers?
questions.targets: Consumer benefits of trade

options.text: A guarantee that no jobs are lost in domestic industries
options.misconception: Trade can cause job losses in industries that compete with imports, so there is no such guarantee.

options.text: Higher prices for imported goods because of transport costs
options.misconception: Transport costs are a cost of trade, not a benefit, and imports are usually cheaper than domestic production.

options.text: A wider choice of goods at lower prices
More tariff revenue collected by the government
options.misconception: Opening up to free trade removes tariffs, and tariff revenue goes to the government, not to consumers.

questions.prompt: Define the term free trade.
hints: Think about what the word 'free' refers to when goods cross borders between countries.
Describe the activity first, then say what is missing from it.
questions.targets: Trade between countries without government restrictions
marking_points: The exchange of goods and services between countries [1]
without government restrictions or intervention, such as tariffs or quotas [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer refers to international exchange and to the absence of government-imposed barriers.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a form of trade protection?
hints: Trade protection gives domestic producers an advantage over foreign producers.
For each option, ask whether it restricts trade or gives local firms an edge, or whether it does the opposite.
questions.targets: Types of trade protection

options.text: A tax on imported cars
options.misconception: A tax on imports is a tariff, the most common form of protection.

options.text: A limit on the quantity of steel that may be imported each year
options.misconception: A quantity limit on imports is an import quota, a form of protection.

options.text: A subsidy paid to domestic firms for each unit they export
options.misconception: Export subsidies give domestic firms an advantage over foreign rivals, so they count as protection.

options.text: A trade agreement that removes tariffs between two countries

questions.prompt: Define the term tariff.
hints: This is the most common form of trade protection; think about what kind of government instrument it is.
State what it is and which goods it applies to.
questions.targets: Tax on imports
marking_points: A tax [1]
imposed on imported goods or services [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer says it is a tax and that it applies to imports; 'a trade barrier' alone earns no marks.

questions.prompt: With the same resources, a worker in Veld can produce more tonnes of rice per day than a worker in Kuva. What can be concluded?
hints: Decide whether the information is about the amount produced or about what is given up.
Only one of the two types of advantage can be judged from output figures for a single good.
questions.targets: Absolute advantage vs comparative advantage

options.text: Veld has a comparative advantage in rice
options.misconception: Comparative advantage depends on opportunity cost, which needs data on another good.

options.text: Veld has an absolute advantage in rice
Veld has a lower opportunity cost of producing rice
options.misconception: Opportunity cost cannot be found without knowing what else each worker could produce.

options.text: Veld has an absolute advantage in all goods
options.misconception: The data only covers rice, so nothing can be said about other goods.

questions.prompt: Define the term specialization.
hints: Think about how a country divides its resources across different products.
Say what the country does with its production and what happens to the range of goods it makes.
questions.targets: Concentrating production on few goods
marking_points: When an individual, firm or country concentrates its production [1]
on one or a few goods or services [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer mentions concentrating production and a narrow range of goods or services.

questions.prompt: A diagram shows the domestic market for steel in Kuva, with domestic demand, domestic supply and a horizontal world supply curve below the domestic equilibrium price. Kuva then imposes a tariff on steel imports. What would the diagram show?
hints: Think about which curve the tariff moves on a tariff diagram.
Read off the new price, then the new quantities supplied by domestic firms and demanded by consumers; imports are the gap between them.
questions.targets: Tariff effects on price, domestic output and imports

options.text: The domestic price rises, domestic production rises and imports fall
The domestic price rises, domestic production falls and imports rise
options.misconception: A higher price makes domestic firms supply more, not less, so imports shrink.

options.text: The world supply curve shifts down and imports rise
options.misconception: A tariff raises the price of imports, so the world supply curve shifts up, not down.

options.text: The domestic price is unchanged and only imports fall
options.misconception: The tariff is added to the world price, so the price paid in Kuva rises.

questions.prompt: Define the term comparative advantage.
hints: Think about how this idea differs from absolute advantage.
Your definition must say what is being compared and between whom.
questions.targets: Lower opportunity cost than another country
marking_points: A country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost [1]
than another country [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Full marks need the idea of lower opportunity cost and a comparison with another country; 'produces more' describes absolute advantage and earns no marks.

questions.prompt: Kuva has almost no oil deposits. Which benefit of international trade is most relevant to Kuva in this case?
hints: Think about the list of benefits of trade and which one relates to natural resources.
Ask what Kuva cannot produce at home and how trade changes that.
questions.targets: Access to resources as a benefit of trade

options.text: The government can collect more tariff revenue
options.misconception: Tariff revenue comes from restricting trade, not from the benefits of free trade.

options.text: Kuva can protect its infant oil industry
options.misconception: Protection is an argument against free trade, and Kuva has no oil to build an industry on.

options.text: Kuva can specialise in producing oil
options.misconception: A country with almost no oil deposits cannot specialise in oil production.

options.text: Kuva can obtain resources that it cannot produce itself

questions.prompt: Using the data in Table 1, calculate the opportunity cost of producing one unit of wheat in Veld and in Kuva, in units of cloth.

table.caption: Table 1: Output per worker per day

hints: Opportunity cost is what must be given up; here it is measured in units of cloth.
For each country, divide the cloth a worker could make by the wheat that worker could make instead.
questions.targets: Opportunity cost ratios from an output table
marking_points: Veld: 4 ÷ 8 = 0.5 units of cloth per unit of wheat [1]
Kuva: 2 ÷ 2 = 1 unit of cloth per unit of wheat [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Full marks need both correct ratios with units of cloth; inverted ratios (2 and 1) earn no marks for Veld.

questions.prompt: Using Table 2, which statement is correct?

table.caption: Table 2: Output per worker per day

hints: Use opportunity cost, not the size of output, to judge comparative advantage.
Work out what each country gives up for one unit of each good, then compare the two countries good by good.
questions.targets: Comparative advantage exists even when one country has absolute advantage in both goods

options.text: Veld has a comparative advantage in both wheat and cloth
options.misconception: Veld produces more of both, which is absolute advantage; a country cannot have a comparative advantage in both goods.

options.text: Veld has a comparative advantage in cloth and Kuva in wheat
options.misconception: This reverses the opportunity cost comparison.

options.text: Veld has a comparative advantage in wheat and Kuva in cloth
Kuva has no comparative advantage because it produces less of both goods
options.misconception: Producing less of both is an absolute disadvantage; Kuva can still have a lower opportunity cost in one good.

questions.prompt: Kuva lost its preferential access to a large export market. Using the data in Table 3, calculate the change in Kuva's export revenue from bananas between 2024 and 2025.
hints: Export revenue is found from the price and the quantity sold abroad.
Find revenue in each year, then subtract the 2024 figure from the 2025 figure and give units.
questions.targets: Export revenue = price × quantity; change with sign and units
marking_points: Revenue 2024 = 6 × 30 = 180 million zeds; revenue 2025 = 5 × 24 = 120 million zeds [1]
Change = 120 − 180 = −60 million zeds (a fall of 60 million zeds) [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Full marks need both revenue figures and a fall of 60 million zeds with units; a missing sign or 'fall' loses the second mark.

questions.prompt: Table 4 shows Veld's coffee exports. What was the percentage change in Veld's coffee export revenue between 2024 and 2025?
hints: Revenue depends on both price and quantity, so work out total revenue first.
Find revenue in each year, then divide the change by the 2024 revenue and multiply by 100.
questions.targets: Percentage change in export revenue, not in price or quantity alone

options.misconception: This is the percentage change in price only, ignoring the rise in quantity.
This is the percentage change in quantity only, ignoring the fall in price.
Adding the price and quantity percentage changes only approximates the change in revenue.

questions.prompt: The world price of rice is 4 zeds per kg. Veld imposes a tariff of 1 zed per kg on rice imports. Using the data in Table 5, calculate the quantity of rice imported after the tariff and the government's tariff revenue.

table.caption: Table 5: Domestic rice market in Veld
columns: Quantity supplied by domestic firms (thousand kg)

hints: Use the row for the price that consumers pay once the tariff is added to the world price.
Imports are the gap between what is demanded and what domestic firms supply; revenue is the tariff per unit times the units imported.
questions.targets: Imports and tariff revenue after a tariff
marking_points: Imports after the tariff = 70 − 40 = 30 thousand kg [1]
Tariff revenue = 1 × 30 = 30 thousand zeds [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Full marks need imports of 30 thousand kg and revenue of 30 thousand zeds; using the free-trade imports (80) earns no marks.

questions.prompt: Kuva imposes an import quota on sugar that is smaller than the quantity it imported under free trade. What is the most likely effect on consumers in Kuva?
hints: Think about a quota diagram, where supply beyond domestic output is limited to a fixed amount.
With fewer imports available, consider what happens to the price and then to the quantity consumers buy.
questions.targets: Import quota raises price and cuts consumption

options.text: They pay the world price and buy more sugar
options.misconception: A quota limits supply, so the domestic price rises above the world price.

options.text: They pay a higher price and buy less sugar
They pay a higher price and buy more sugar
options.misconception: With a downward-sloping demand curve, a higher price reduces the quantity demanded.

options.text: The price is unchanged but consumers pay a tax to the government
options.misconception: A quota is a quantity limit, not a tax; the price rises and the government gets no revenue unless it sells licences.

questions.prompt: Using the data in Table 6, explain which good each country should specialise in.

table.caption: Table 6: Output per worker per day

hints: Specialisation should follow comparative advantage, so you need opportunity costs, not output levels.
Work out what each country gives up for one phone and for one tonne of rice, compare them, and match each country to the good with the lower cost.
questions.targets: Applying comparative advantage when one country has absolute advantage in both
marking_points: Opportunity cost of one phone: Veld 20 ÷ 10 = 2 tonnes of rice; Kuva 12 ÷ 4 = 3 tonnes of rice [1]
Veld has the lower opportunity cost of phones, so it should specialise in phones [1]
Opportunity cost of one tonne of rice: Kuva 1/3 phone vs Veld 1/2 phone, so Kuva should specialise in rice [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer uses opportunity cost figures for both countries and assigns phones to Veld and rice to Kuva; answers based only on Veld producing more earn 0.

questions.prompt: Veld and Kuva each have a straight-line production possibilities curve (PPC), with wheat on the horizontal axis and cloth on the vertical axis. Veld's PPC is steeper than Kuva's. What can be concluded?
hints: The slope of a straight-line PPC shows an opportunity cost.
Work out what a steeper slope means for the cloth given up per unit of wheat, then decide which good is relatively cheaper for Veld.
questions.targets: Reading comparative advantage from PPC slopes

options.text: Veld has a comparative advantage in cloth
Veld has a comparative advantage in wheat
options.misconception: A steeper slope means Veld gives up more cloth per unit of wheat, so wheat is relatively costly for Veld.

options.text: Veld has an absolute advantage in both goods
options.misconception: Absolute advantage depends on where the PPC is, not on its slope.

options.text: Neither country can gain from trade
options.misconception: Gains are impossible only if the slopes are equal; different slopes mean different opportunity costs.

questions.prompt: The world price of rice is 4 zeds per kg. Veld imposes a tariff of 1 zed per kg on rice imports. Using the data in Table 7, calculate the change in the revenue of domestic rice producers.

table.caption: Table 7: Domestic rice market in Veld
columns: Quantity supplied by domestic firms (thousand kg)

hints: Producer revenue uses the price domestic firms receive and the quantity they sell.
Find domestic producers' revenue at the world price and at the price with the tariff, then find the difference.
questions.targets: Domestic producer revenue before and after a tariff
marking_points: Before: 4 × 20 = 80 thousand zeds; after: 5 × 40 = 200 thousand zeds [1]
Change = 200 − 80 = an increase of 120 thousand zeds [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Full marks need both revenue figures and an increase of 120 thousand zeds; using quantity demanded instead of domestic supply earns no marks.

questions.prompt: Veld specialises according to its comparative advantage and trades with Kuva on terms that benefit both countries. On a diagram of Veld's PPC, where can Veld's consumption point now be?
hints: Distinguish between what Veld can produce and what Veld can consume once it trades.
Think about what Veld receives in exchange for its exports compared with what it would give up producing those goods itself.
questions.targets: Gains from trade: consumption beyond the PPC

options.text: On a new PPC further out, because trade increases Veld's resources
options.misconception: Trade does not change the quantity of Veld's factors of production, so the PPC itself does not shift.

options.text: Inside its PPC
options.misconception: A point inside the PPC means unused resources or a loss, not a gain from trade.

options.text: On its PPC, with more of both goods than before
options.misconception: Moving along a PPC always means giving up some of one good to get more of the other.

options.text: Outside its PPC

questions.prompt: Explain how free trade can increase the efficiency of domestic firms in Veld.
hints: Think about the competition domestic firms face once foreign goods can enter freely.
Link that competition to firms' costs and behaviour, then to how the country's resources are used.
questions.targets: Competition from trade and efficiency
marking_points: Domestic firms face more competition from foreign producers [1]
so they must cut costs, improve quality or innovate, and inefficient firms may leave the market [1]
resources move to more productive uses, lowering costs and prices / improving allocative efficiency [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer links foreign competition to pressure on firms and then to better use of resources or lower costs and prices.

questions.prompt: The world price of rice is 4 zeds per kg and Veld imposes a tariff of 1 zed per kg. The domestic supply curve is a straight line. Using Table 8, by how much does domestic producer surplus increase?

table.caption: Table 8: Domestic rice market in Veld
columns: Quantity supplied by domestic firms (thousand kg)

hints: On a tariff diagram, the gain in producer surplus is the area between the two prices, to the left of the domestic supply curve.
That area is a trapezium: use the average of the two domestic quantities multiplied by the price change.
questions.targets: Producer surplus change vs revenue change

options.text: 20 thousand zeds
options.misconception: This is only the change in domestic output multiplied by the tariff, which misses the rectangle for existing output.

options.text: 120 thousand zeds
options.misconception: This is the change in producer revenue, which includes the costs of producing the extra output.

options.text: 30 thousand zeds
60 thousand zeds
options.misconception: This adds the two quantities without averaging them, so the trapezium is counted twice.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between absolute advantage and comparative advantage.
hints: One concept is judged by output levels and the other by what is given up.
Write one clear sentence for each concept, making the basis of comparison explicit.
questions.targets: Output with the same resources vs opportunity cost
marking_points: Absolute advantage: a country can produce more of a good than another country with the same resources (or use fewer resources) [1]
Comparative advantage: a country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Both concepts must be explained with the correct basis (resources/output vs opportunity cost); two definitions without a comparison with another country lose marks.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a reason why the gains from trade predicted by the theory of comparative advantage may not be achieved in practice?
hints: Think about the simplifying assumptions behind the theory of comparative advantage.
Separate the conditions that create gains from the real-world factors that can cancel them out.
questions.targets: Limitations of comparative advantage theory

options.text: Countries have different opportunity costs
options.misconception: Different opportunity costs are what create the gains from trade in the first place.

options.text: Transport costs may be larger than the difference in opportunity costs
Countries trade at terms between their two opportunity costs
options.misconception: Trading between the two opportunity costs is the condition for both countries to gain.

options.text: Specialisation increases total world output
options.misconception: Higher total output is a gain from specialisation, not a limitation.

questions.prompt: Veld currently has a tariff of 1 zed per kg on rice, and the world price is 4 zeds per kg. The demand and domestic supply curves are straight lines. Using the data in Table 9, calculate the gain in social welfare if Veld removes the tariff.

table.caption: Table 9: Domestic rice market in Veld
columns: Quantity supplied by domestic firms (thousand kg)

hints: Removing the tariff gets rid of the deadweight loss it caused; on a tariff diagram this loss is two triangles.
Find one triangle from the change in domestic supply and one from the change in quantity demanded, each with the tariff as its height, then add them.
questions.targets: Welfare loss of a tariff: production and consumption triangles
marking_points: Production-side triangle = ½ × (40 − 20) × 1 = 10 thousand zeds [1]
Consumption-side triangle = ½ × (100 − 70) × 1 = 15 thousand zeds [1]
Gain in social welfare = 10 + 15 = 25 thousand zeds [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Full marks need both triangles and a total of 25 thousand zeds; forgetting the ½ (answer 50) loses the final mark only if the method is otherwise correct.

questions.prompt: Veld imports much of its steel at the world price. The government gives domestic steel producers a subsidy per tonne produced. What would a diagram of Veld's steel market show?
hints: Think about which curve the subsidy shifts and whether the price paid by consumers is still set by the world price.
Compare the new domestic output with total demand to find what happens to imports.
questions.targets: Production subsidy vs tariff: price unchanged, imports fall

options.text: The domestic price rises above the world price and consumption falls
options.misconception: This describes a tariff; a subsidy lowers producers' costs without raising the price consumers pay.

options.text: The domestic price falls below the world price and imports rise
options.misconception: The price stays at the world price, because consumers can still buy imports at that price.

options.text: Domestic production rises and imports also rise
options.misconception: With consumption unchanged, more domestic output must replace some imports.

options.text: The price stays at the world price, domestic production rises and imports fall

questions.prompt: Explain one reason, other than transport costs, why a country may not gain as much as the theory of comparative advantage predicts.
hints: Think about the other simplifying assumptions of the theory, such as those about costs or about how easily resources move.
State the assumption that fails in reality, then say how that failure reduces the gains.
questions.targets: Limitations of comparative advantage (costs, factor mobility, risks)
marking_points: Identifies an unrealistic assumption or real-world problem, e.g. rising costs as output expands, immobile factors of production, or over-dependence on a few exports [1]
Explains how it reduces the gains, e.g. opportunity costs rise with specialisation, workers in shrinking industries become unemployed, or export earnings become unstable [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer names one valid limitation other than transport costs and clearly explains why it reduces the gains from specialisation.

questions.prompt: Under free trade, Veld can buy rice at the world price of 4 zeds per kg. Using Table 10, what are total consumer spending on rice and the quantity of rice imported?

table.caption: Table 10: Domestic rice market in Veld
columns: Quantity supplied by domestic firms (thousand kg)

hints: Use only the row for the world price, since there is no tariff.
Spending uses the quantity consumers buy; imports are the part of that quantity not supplied by domestic firms.
questions.targets: Consumer spending and imports at the world price

options.text: Spending 400 thousand zeds; imports 80 thousand kg
Spending 400 thousand zeds; imports 100 thousand kg
options.misconception: Not all rice is imported; domestic firms still supply part of the quantity demanded.

options.text: Spending 80 thousand zeds; imports 20 thousand kg
options.misconception: These use the domestic supply figure, which describes domestic producers, not consumers or imports.

options.text: Spending 320 thousand zeds; imports 80 thousand kg
options.misconception: This counts only spending on imports, not total consumer spending on rice.

questions.prompt: Explain how access to international markets can allow firms in Kuva to lower their average costs.
hints: Think about the concept that links the scale of production to average costs.
Link the size of the market firms can sell to, to the amount they produce, and then to their costs per unit.
questions.targets: Trade, larger markets and economies of scale
marking_points: Trade gives firms access to a much larger market than the domestic one [1]
so firms can expand and produce on a larger scale [1]
gaining economies of scale, so average (unit) costs fall [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer links a bigger market to larger-scale production and to economies of scale that reduce average costs.

questions.prompt: Using Table 11, Veld specialises in wheat and exports it to Kuva in exchange for cloth. Which terms of trade would benefit both countries?

table.caption: Table 11: Output per worker per day

hints: Mutually beneficial terms of trade lie between the two countries' opportunity costs of the traded good.
Find each country's opportunity cost of one unit of wheat in cloth, then pick the option that falls between them.
questions.targets: Terms of trade must lie between the opportunity cost ratios

options.text: 1 unit of wheat for 0.25 units of cloth
options.misconception: Veld could get more cloth than this by moving its own resources out of wheat, so Veld would lose.

options.text: 1 unit of wheat for 0.75 units of cloth
1 unit of wheat for 1.5 units of cloth
options.misconception: Kuva gives up only 1 unit of cloth to make a unit of wheat itself, so it would not pay more.

options.text: 1 unit of wheat for 2 units of cloth
options.misconception: This uses the inverted ratio (Veld's opportunity cost of cloth in wheat) and Kuva would not accept it.

questions.prompt: Veld signs a trade agreement that removes its tariff on imported shoes. Explain, with reference to a tariff diagram, the effects on consumers, domestic shoe producers and imports in Veld.
hints: Use a diagram with domestic demand, domestic supply and a world supply curve that moves when the tariff goes.
Start with the new price, then read off what happens to the quantity bought, the quantity made at home and the gap between them.
questions.targets: Effects of tariff removal on price, consumer and producer surplus, and imports
marking_points: The domestic price falls to the world price [1]
consumers buy more at the lower price, so consumer surplus rises [1]
domestic producers supply less, so their revenue/producer surplus falls [1]
imports rise, as the gap between quantity demanded and domestic supply widens [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer covers the fall in price and the separate effects on consumers, domestic producers and imports, each linked to the diagram.
